title: Estimating before you calculate
objectives: Round a number to one significant figure
Estimate a calculation in your head and use it to check an answer

screens.prose: A spreadsheet cell says $48 \times 21 = 10{,}080$. The point marks that answer on the line.
screens.question: Is the spreadsheet's answer plausible?

options.why: You trusted the digits. $50 \times 20$ is only 1,000, ten times smaller.
$50 \times 20 = 1{,}000$, not 100. $5 \times 2 = 10$, then add two more zeros.

hints.text: 48 is close to 50, and 21 is close to 20.
The point sits near 10,000. Compare it with $50 \times 20$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Replace 48 and 21 with nearby round numbers and multiply.

explain.text: $48 \approx 50$ and $21 \approx 20$, so the product is near $50 \times 20 = 1{,}000$. The true answer is 1,008; the spreadsheet has an extra 0. A rough estimate caught it.

screens.prose: Rounding swaps a number for a nearby round one. The line runs from 0 to 1,000 in hundreds. Drag the blue point; it snaps to the hundreds.
screens.question: Drag the point to 387 rounded to the nearest hundred.

hints.text: Which hundreds sit either side of 387?
387 is between 300 and 400. Which is nearer?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the hundred nearest to 387.

byKey.truncated: You dropped the digits after the 3. But 387 is nearer 400 than 300.
byKey.ten-times: Move the point. It starts at 0; drag it to the hundred nearest 387.

explain.text: 387 sits 13 below 400 and 87 above 300. Rounding picks the nearer hundred, 400. Only the first digit survives, rounded, and zeros hold its place.

screens.prose: You kept one non-zero digit, rounded, and filled the rest with zeros. That is rounding to **one significant figure**: 387 becomes 400. Leading zeros never count as significant.
screens.question: Round 0.0372 to one significant figure.

options.why: You rounded to the nearest whole number. The first significant figure is the 3, the first non-zero digit.
You cut off the digits after the 3. The next digit is 7, so the 3 rounds up.
That keeps two significant figures, 3 and 7. Keep only one.

hints.text: Which is the first non-zero digit?
The point sits between 0.03 and 0.04. Which is nearer?
The 3 is followed by a 7, so it rounds up to 4.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the first non-zero digit, then round it using the digit after.

explain.text: Leading zeros only hold the place, so the first significant figure is the 3. The next digit, 7, rounds it up to 4. On the line, 0.0372 is nearer 0.04 than 0.03.

screens.prose: Now estimate a product. Round each number to one significant figure and multiply in your head. Then drag the point to your estimate.
screens.question: Estimate $312 \times 48$.

hints.text: Round 312 and 48 to one significant figure.
312 becomes 300 and 48 becomes 50.
$3 \times 5 = 15$, then put back the three zeros.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Round each number to one significant figure, then multiply.

byKey.rounded-down: You rounded 48 down to 40. 48 is nearer 50.
byKey.lost-zero: You lost a zero. $300 \times 50$ is $3 \times 5$ followed by three zeros.

explain.text: $312 \approx 300$ and $48 \approx 50$, so the estimate is $300 \times 50 = 15{,}000$. The exact product is 14,976, very close. Speed matters here, not precision.

screens.prose: Estimate $612 \div 0.48$. Rounded to one significant figure, that is $600 \div 0.5$.
screens.question: Which estimate is right?

options.why: You halved 600. Dividing by 0.5 asks how many halves fit in 600, and 1,200 do.
You lost a zero. $600 \div 0.5$ is the same as $6{,}000 \div 5$.
You ignored the 0.5. Dividing by a number below 1 changes the answer; it grows.

hints.text: How many halves fit in 1? How many in 600?
Two halves fit in every 1.
$600 \times 2 = 1{,}200$ halves fit in 600.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask how many lots of 0.5 fit into 600.

byKey.halved: You halved 600. Dividing by 0.5 is not halving: it counts the halves, and there are 1,200.

explain.text: Dividing by 0.5 counts how many halves fit, and 600 holds 1,200 of them. Dividing by a number below 1 makes the answer bigger. The exact answer is 1,275.

screens.prose: Three numbers now. Round each to one significant figure, estimate $\dfrac{38.7 \times 5.12}{0.198}$, then drag the point to your estimate.
screens.question: Where does your estimate land?

hints.text: Round 38.7, 5.12 and 0.198 to one significant figure.
They become 40, 5 and 0.2.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Round all three numbers, then work out the top before dividing.

byKey.top-only: That is the top alone, $40 \times 5$. Now divide by 0.2, which makes it bigger.
byKey.lost-zero: You lost a zero. $200 \div 0.2$ is the same as $2{,}000 \div 2$.

explain.text: Rounded, the calculation is $\dfrac{40 \times 5}{0.2} = \dfrac{200}{0.2} = 1{,}000$. The exact value is about 1,000.7. Rounding errors in the top and bottom partly cancelled.

screens.prose: Code returns three candidates for $312 \times 48$. You estimated 15,000. The bars show all four numbers.
screens.question: Which candidate can be right?

options.why: A is ten times smaller than the estimate. A slipped decimal point would do this.
C is ten times bigger than 15,000. An extra digit crept in.

hints.text: Which bar is about as tall as the estimate?
Compare each candidate with 15,000.
Only one candidate is within a factor of 2 of 15,000.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare each candidate with the estimate.

explain.text: B sits right beside the estimate. A is ten times too small and C is ten times too big. An estimate cannot pick the digits, but it rules out the wrong size.

screens.prose: Every time you did the same thing. Round each number to one significant figure, then calculate: $$48 \times 21 \approx 50 \times 20 = 1{,}000$$ If the real answer is about ten times off the estimate, a digit or a decimal point has slipped.
screens.question: Estimate $0.62 \times 0.38$.

options.why: Count the decimal places: $0.6 \times 0.4$ has two, so the answer is 0.24.
One decimal place each makes two in the answer, not three.
You multiplied 6 by 4 and dropped the decimal points. Both numbers are below 1, so the answer is too.

hints.text: Round each number to one significant figure.
$0.6 \times 0.4$: $6 \times 4 = 24$, then two decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Round, multiply the digits, then place the decimal point.

explain.text: Rounded, it is $0.6 \times 0.4$. The digits give $6 \times 4 = 24$, and two decimal places make 0.24. The exact product is 0.2356.

screens.prose: A trade ticket says $\text{£}23.80 \times 395 = \text{£}94{,}010$. Check it in your head.
screens.question: Put the steps of the check in order.

lines.text: Round to one significant figure: £20 and 400
Compare: £94,010 is more than ten times the estimate
So the ticket is wrong; the true total is £9,401

hints.text: What do you do before any multiplying?
Round first, then multiply the round numbers.
Round, multiply, compare, conclude.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. You need the estimate before you can compare.

byKey.multiply: You multiply the rounded numbers, so rounding comes first.
byKey.compare: Comparing needs the estimate, so it comes after the multiplication.
byKey.conclude: The verdict comes last, after the comparison.

explain.text: $\text{£}23.80 \approx \text{£}20$ and $395 \approx 400$, so the total is near £8,000. £94,010 is more than ten times that, so a digit slipped. The exact total is £9,401.

screens.prose: A backtest log reports 2,150 trades with an average profit of £0.38 each. It gives the total profit as £8,170.
screens.question: What should the total be, roughly?

options.why: You agreed with the log. $2{,}000 \times 0.4$ is 800, so the log is ten times too big.
$2{,}000 \times 0.4 = 800$. You dropped a zero.
You divided 2,000 by 0.4. The total is trades times profit per trade.

hints.text: Round 2,150 and £0.38 to one significant figure.
They become 2,000 and £0.4.

feedback.correct: $2{,}000 \times \text{£}0.4 = \text{£}800$: the log is ten times too big.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Round both numbers and multiply.

explain.text: $2{,}150 \approx 2{,}000$ and $\text{£}0.38 \approx \text{£}0.4$, so the total is near $2{,}000 \times 0.4 = \text{£}800$. The exact product is £817, so the log has a slipped decimal point. A ten-times error is exactly what an estimate catches.

ideas: Round to one significant figure: keep the first non-zero digit, rounded, and hold the place with zeros.
Estimate first, calculate second, then compare: a gap of about ten times means a slipped digit or decimal point.
Dividing by a number below 1 makes the answer bigger: $600 \div 0.5 = 1{,}200$.

formula.name: Estimate with one significant figure
formula.note: The estimate is for checking. Keep the exact answer for reporting.

summary.trap: Dividing by 0.5 doubles a number; it does not halve it.

options.why: You cut off the digits after the 5. The next digit is 8, so round up.
You rounded to two decimal places. The first significant figure is the 5.
That keeps two significant figures. Keep only one.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the first non-zero digit, then round it.

explain.text: The first non-zero digit is 5, and the 8 after it rounds it up. So 0.00586 becomes 0.006.

quiz.prose: Round each number to one significant figure.
quiz.question: Estimate $59 \times 312$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Round to 60 and 300, then multiply.

byKey.rounded-down: You rounded 59 down to 50. 59 is nearer 60.
byKey.lost-zero: You lost a zero. $60 \times 300$ ends in three zeros.
byKey.exact: That is the exact product. Round first: $60 \times 300$.

explain.text: $59 \approx 60$ and $312 \approx 300$. So the estimate is $60 \times 300 = 18{,}000$; the exact product is 18,408.

quiz.prose: Round each number to one significant figure.
quiz.question: Estimate $\dfrac{4{,}120}{0.21}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask how many lots of 0.2 fit in 4,000.

byKey.multiplied: You multiplied by 0.2. Dividing by 0.2 makes the answer bigger: five lots of 0.2 fit in each 1.

explain.text: $4{,}120 \approx 4{,}000$ and $0.21 \approx 0.2$. Five lots of 0.2 fit in each 1, so $4{,}000 \div 0.2 = 20{,}000$. The exact value is about 19,619.

quiz.prose: Rounding can carry into a new digit.
quiz.question: Round 96 to one significant figure.

options.why: You cut off the 6. The 6 rounds the 9 up, which carries into the hundreds.
Rounding keeps place value: 96 is near 100, not near 10.
That moves the decimal point. Rounding keeps the size of the number.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the nearest number with one non-zero digit.

explain.text: The 6 rounds the 9 up to 10, which carries: 96 becomes 100. This is the edge case where the rounded number gains a digit.

quiz.prose: A risk report values a position of 4,900 shares at £19.70 each as £965,300.
quiz.question: Is the value plausible?

options.why: You trusted the digits. $5{,}000 \times 20 = 100{,}000$, so the report is ten times too big.
$5{,}000 \times 20 = 100{,}000$. You dropped a zero.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Round both numbers and multiply.

explain.text: $4{,}900 \approx 5{,}000$ and $\text{£}19.70 \approx \text{£}20$, so the position is near £100,000. The exact value is £96,530: the report has an extra digit.
